questions.q: Define "collocation" and give one example from the chapter "Discovering Tut" that is NOT "funerary treasures".
questions.a: A collocation is a predictable, habitual co-occurrence of two or more words that sounds natural to native speakers (e.g., "ritual resins", "dark-bellied clouds", "scientific detachment"). A wrong answer (e.g., "any adjective+noun pair like 'big tomb'") reveals the student confuses free combination with fixed collocation — they cannot distinguish "stunning artefacts" (strong collocation) from "beautiful artefacts" (free combination).

questions.q: Explain why the author chooses "casket grey" instead of "dark grey" or "coffin grey" to describe the sky. What semantic nuance does this collocation add?
questions.a: "Casket grey" fuses the colour of the sky with the funerary context of the Valley of the Kings, foreshadowing Tut's death and the CT scan's clinical examination. "Dark grey" is neutral; "coffin grey" is possible but "casket" carries stronger associations with viewing/burial rituals. A wrong answer focusing only on colour description misses the intertextual echo with "casket" in "funerary treasures" and the motif of death that structures the passage.

questions.q: Classify the following terms by their morphological structure and register: tomography, autopsy, biopsy, angiography. Identify the Greek root in each and its literal meaning.
questions.a: All are medical register terms from Greek: tomography (tomos "slice" + graphein "write"), autopsy (autos "self" + opsis "seeing"), biopsy (bios "life" + opsis), angiography (angeion "vessel" + graphein). Steps: (1) segment each word, (2) identify Greek roots, (3) translate roots, (4) note all end in -y/-graphy indicating process/recording. A wrong answer listing only definitions without morphology shows inability to decode technical vocabulary systematically — a critical skill for Class 11 science/English crossover.

questions.q: Compare the collocations "ghostly dust devils" and "virtual body". How does each reflect a different register (literary vs. scientific) and what does their coexistence reveal about the text's hybrid genre?
questions.a: "Ghostly dust devils" belongs to literary/gothic register (supernatural modifier + natural phenomenon), creating eerie atmosphere. "Virtual body" belongs to scientific/technological register (computing metaphor + anatomy), signalling digital precision. Their coexistence mirrors the text's hybrid genre: part travelogue, part forensic report. A wrong answer treating both as "descriptive phrases" misses the register clash that embodies the central tension — ancient mystery vs. modern technology.

questions.q: Evaluate the claim: "Languages die only when their last speaker dies." Use the Egyptian/Coptic trajectory from the text and one Indian example to support or refute.
questions.a: The claim is false. Egyptian did not vanish with the last speaker; it evolved into Coptic (2nd century CE), which survived as a liturgical language until the 19th century and is still used ritually. Similarly, Sanskrit lost native speakers centuries ago but persists in rituals, scholarship, and revived spoken communities. Language death is a process of domain shrinkage (administration, education, media), not a single event. A wrong answer equating "extinct" with "no speakers" ignores the text's explicit timeline: "Coptic may still have been used as late as the early nineteenth century and is still used as a religious language".

questions.q: Create a 4-line stanza using at least three collocations from the chapter (e.g., "eternal brilliance", "ritual resins", "dark-bellied clouds") that reimagines the CT scan scene from the mummy's perspective.
questions.a:
*Beneath dark-bellied clouds I wake,*
*Eternal brilliance scans my frame,*
*Ritual resins hold the ache,*
*Virtual body speaks my name.*
Criteria: (1) three collocations used accurately, (2) consistent perspective, (3) poetic compression. A poor answer uses collocations as decorative fillers without integrating them into a coherent voice — showing they are memorised chunks, not productive linguistic resources.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Language usage in the text?
questions.a: Students treat "Working with Words" as a vocabulary list to memorise rather than a linguistic analysis task.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to (1) identify and explain the semantic effect of 5+ adjectival-noun collocations from the text, (2) classify and define 5+ medical/scientific terms by register and function, and (3) articulate reasons for language extinction and preservation strategies using textual evidence and real-world examples.
